extracted.intended_audience: general encyclopedia readers, students and researchers of American humor and literary/film comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize the stylistic devices, recurring characters, formats, and topical approaches that define Robert Benchley's humor across essays, columns, stage acts, and short films. Useful for studying or emulating Benchley's brand of early 20th-century American literary and performance comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre labels: deadpan, parody, surreal humor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchley is described in the infobox and throughout as working in deadpan delivery, parody pieces, and occasional surreal humor; these genre labels frame both his written essays and short films (e.g., mock-instructional lectures such as How to Sleep).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchley's definition of humor was simple: "Anything that makes people laugh."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows a pragmatic, audience-centered yardstick: the primary evaluative goal is eliciting laughter rather than adhering to a stricter ideological or literary standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Little Man' / common-man protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchley's characters were typically exaggerated representations of the common man. They were designed to create a contrast between himself and the masses; the character is often befuddled by society and is often neurotic in a "different" way — the character in How to Watch Football, for instance, finds it sensible for a normal fan to forgo the live experience and read the recap in the local papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recurring persona ('Little Man') is a central comic device across formats (essays, speaking, acting). Use of an everyman who is confounded or inept is a hallmark; in performance, exaggeration of mannerisms and nervousness (e.g., The Treasurer's Report) is encouraged. Note: the Little Man persisted more in his speaking/acting roles than in later written pieces after the early 1930s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on puns and wordplay (literary humorist orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lampoon primarily used the latter [genteel] style, which suited Benchley. While some of his pieces would not have been out of place in a crackerbarrel-style presentation, Benchley's reliance on puns and wordplay resonated more with the literary humorists, as shown by his success with The New Yorker, known for the highbrow tastes of its readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize clever language, puns, and subtle wordplay appropriate to a literate/newspaper-magazine audience rather than broad dialect comedic devices. This stylistic choice aligns work with 'genteel' literary humor rather than down-market crackerbarrel comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical/current-event pieces that retain levity
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical, current-event style pieces written for Vanity Fair during the war did not lose their levity, either. He was not afraid to poke fun at the establishment (one piece he wrote was titled "Have You a Little German Agent in Your Home?"), and his common man observations often veered into angry rants, such as his piece "The Average Voter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing topical satire, maintain humorous tone even while addressing serious or political subjects; use analogies (e.g., football and patriotism) and exaggeration to lampoon institutions without losing the comic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-instructional/lecture format
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchley's screen image was established as a comic lecturer who tried but failed to clarify any given topic. His short movie series featured mock-instructional lectures (How to Sleep, How to Be a Detective, How to Rest) or situations where he coped awkwardly with household matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The faux-authoritative lecture—deadpan delivery giving absurd 'instructions'—is a proven effective format for short comedy; juxtapose formal instructional tone with ridiculous content and let the speaker's failure create humor. Suitable for short-subject films and staged monologues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting the commonplace as remarkable
rubrics_metrics.description: James Thurber cited Benchley's penchant for presenting "the commonplace as remarkable" in 'The Secret Life of Walter Mitty'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplify mundane details into absurd significance; treating ordinary events with overblown seriousness generates comedic contrast. This is a technique evident in essays and spoken sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration of mundanity / being overmatched by simple tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer, plot-driven shorts... show a Benchley character overmatched by seemingly mundane tasks. Even the more stereotypical characters held these qualities, such as the incapable sportscaster Benchley played in The Sport Parade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create scenarios where trivial tasks balloon into insurmountable obstacles for the protagonist; comedic tension arises from the mismatch between task simplicity and character incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humor to publicize social/petty grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: His reviews were known for their flair, and he often used them to publicise issues of concern to him, whether petty (people who cough during plays) or more important (such as racial intolerance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can function as social criticism; embedding commentary about social norms or injustices within a comedic frame can highlight issues while keeping reader engagement. Balance satire of petty matters with sharper commentary when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genteel vs crackerbarrel stylistic axis
rubrics_metrics.description: The prominent styles of humor were then 'crackerbarrel'—which relied on devices such as dialects and a disdain for formal education—and a more 'genteel' style of humor, very literary and upper-class in nature. The Lampoon primarily used the latter style, which suited Benchley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling Benchley, prefer the 'genteel' literary tone (subtlety, wordplay, upper-class sensibility) rather than populist dialect-based comedy. Choosing this axis determines diction, audience assumptions, and comedic targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-subject film format and production constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchley's short movies were often about 10 minutes in length; How to Sleep was filmed in two days and later shorts were produced even faster (How to Vote needed less than twelve hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For producing similar material, favor concise setups and tight pacing suitable for one-reel/10-minute shorts; the mock-lecture or single-situation premise is well-suited to rapid production and short runtimes. Quick shooting schedules require scripts that rely on a single strong comic conceit.
